newsitem.title: USA: Falling corn prices spark gains in feeder cattle.
newsitem.headline: Falling corn prices spark gains in feeder cattle.

text.p: Falling corn prices and profitable cattle prices have feedlots filling pens with young animals and pushed Chicago Mercantile Exchange feeder cattle futures to 12-month highs, with more gains likely, analysts said.

CME November feeder cattle futures closed Monday at 64.725 cents per lb, up 0.150 cent from Friday, and some analysts predict the contract could reach 66.00 to 67.00 cents before its expiration November 21.

A number of factors are driving the demand for feeder cattle, sources said. Feedlots are earning $85 to $90 per head profits on slaughter cattle and corn prices have fallen nearly $3.00 per bushel since July.
"It is giving clear signals to place cattle," said Karl Skold, director of research at Frontier Risk Management, of the current market conditions.
Also, analysts estimate that feedlots can lock in profits of $50 to $80 per head by hedging purchases of feeder cattle and corn on the CME and Chicago Board of Trade futures markets.
Cattle feeders also may be hedging sales of market-ready cattle against deferred CME live cattle.
Dale Benson, analyst with Dean Witter Reynolds, expects further gains in live cattle futures, which should pull feeder cattle prices up as well.
"I think the (nearby live cattle futures) market is susceptible to very strong rally, which could bring the deferreds up as well," Benson said.
He said CME December live cattle could climb to 71.00 to 73.00 cents per lb soon, which would boost deferred contracts as well. December live cattle closed Monday at 67.525 cents.
Also driving the feeder cattle markets is the abundance of feed. Wheat pastures are lush and feedlots are finding ample supplies of corn and sorghum.

"The huge quantity of feed in the cattle feeding areas has people excited," said Paul Georgy, livestock analyst and president of Allendale Inc. "I guess they (feeder cattle markets) still have room for a couple of dollars (per cwt) higher."
The lush pastures have ranchers grazing cattle rather than selling them to feedlots, said Tom Tippens, chief executive officer of Professional Cattle Consultants.

"I think in the longer term, the feeder market will continue to strengthen as feed prices go down," he said. "I think the general trend is to the high 60s (cents per lb), with the potential to the 70s."
